The finding

Can you tell whether a first-order logic formula says what its sentence says, with no gold formula to compare against?

Ask several independent LLM families to translate the same sentence. Then count how many of those translations a proves equivalent to the candidate, after lining up predicate names. The share that disagree is the . Correct translations tend to agree with each other; wrong ones scatter.

In a test on 2,686 real candidates for 292 sentences (), consensus beat the prompted Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite judge on by

Dataset E was frozen before this test but later reused for metric selection, so the paper treats these as development-set results. The matching test on the fresh set E2 was stopped by budget.

      Five real cases of this failure

        What the paper does not show

        • Renaming breaks the aligner. The name-similarity aligner fails on synonym substitutions and nonce renamings: false-alarm rates rise from 0.18 to 0.87 under WordNet-synonym renaming on dataset E. Name-free alignment lowers AUROC by 0.05 to 0.10 because it over-accepts granularity differences. The paper calls this the method's most significant open weakness.
        • Errors every family makes are invisible. About 12.4% of erroneous translations on dataset E are endorsed by a majority of peers (e = 0.124). Consensus cannot detect them by definition.
        • No advantage on short sentences. On the CTRL stratum the delta against the judge is −0.069 [−0.232, +0.098].
        • Labels move the numbers. The consensus-vs-judge delta shifts by 0.02 to 0.10 depending on whether labels come from the solver alone, the solver plus panel, or all tiers.
        • The panel is strict. It accepts only 61% of expert-corrected formulas and rejects 82% of MALLS gold annotations, so ERROR is over-called.
        • Confirmation on fresh data is partial. The pre-registered E2 test was budget-stopped after 110 of 550 sentences. On that prefix consensus ties a local 8B judge (0.890 vs 0.913, delta +0.003 [−0.042, +0.052]).
